turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_toughness_pareto_train.csv: 300 real steels,
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1
    time, Heat treatment step 1 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2
    temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2 cooling
    rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time,
    Heat treatment step 3 cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 3 time, Secondary treatment step 4
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and the two measured objectives
    `yield strength (MPa)` and `toughness (J)` (both at room temperature).
  - b3_htsteel_toughness_pareto_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE steels whose
    objectives were NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same
    process/composition columns.

Select 5 candidates that jointly span the best trade-off between HIGH yield
strength (MPa) and HIGH toughness (J). Neither objective is given for the
pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated hypervolume they span in the
normalized (yield strength (MPa), toughness (J)) plane, so a set of mutually
non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5 candidates that are
all strong on one axis only.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit list of
candidate_ids, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
I would select a toughness anchor, a strength anchor, and three candidates with plausible intermediate trade-offs. This avoids concentrating all five picks in the high-strength, low-toughness region.

| Candidate | Intended role | Evidence from the training data |
|---|---|---|
| **c010** | High-toughness anchor | Its closest composition/process analogue—23.5% Cr, 27.5% Ni, 2.75% Mo and 3% Cu, solution-treated at 1050°C—achieved **270 MPa and 350 J**. The composition changes introduce uncertainty, but this is a strong toughness-end candidate. |
| **c049** | Toughness-to-strength bridge | The same composition, solution-treated at 880°C and subsequently aged at 650°C, achieved **800 MPa and 168 J**; aging at 550°C produced **1184 MPa and 100 J**. Omitting aging makes c049 a less certain pick, but potentially shifts it toward greater toughness and intermediate strength. |
| **c085** | Central frontier candidate | Very close three-step-treatment analogues achieved **710 MPa / 230 J** with a final 680°C step and **780 MPa / 120 J** at 650°C. Its 675°C final step makes it particularly attractive for the middle of the frontier, although the longer holding time matters. |
| **c044** | Higher-strength intermediate | The identical composition achieved **1000 MPa and 100 J** under a different solution-and-aging schedule. Related Ti-strengthened, Ni-rich steels also support a useful intermediate trade-off. Its precise performance is less certain because the treatment differs. |
| **c041** | High-strength anchor | Identical-composition training steels achieved **1330 MPa / 60 J** at 300°C tempering, **1340 MPa / 61 J** at 400°C, and **1090 MPa / 88 J** at 550°C. The proposed 450°C temper lies within this well-supported high-strength region. |

These are **inferred trade-off roles, not measured pool outcomes**. The strongest local evidence supports c010, c085 and c041; c049 and c044 provide intermediate coverage with greater treatment-related uncertainty.

Final: c010, c049, c085, c044, c041
